name: Schnupperklettern an der Martinswand
beschreibung:
Overview
The prominent Martinswand, rising sheer for over six hundred meters above the Inntal valley near Zirl just west of Innsbruck, ranks among the most storied climbing cliffs in the Alps. Steeped in history since Emperor Maximilian I's legendary rescue, the limestone bastion today offers a world-class rock climbing haven. While sheer upper tiers like the Dschungelbuch challenge international elites, the base of the wall hosts the dedicated ÖAV Climbing Garden and the gently angled Schleicherplatten slabs—creating an ideal outdoor classroom for novices. Guided by certified mountain guides and Alpine Club instructors, beginner taster sessions introduce climbers to the fundamentals of vertical rock climbing with absolute safety.

Route & Requirements
The instructional climbing area focuses on two beginner-friendly sectors:
1. Schleicherplatten: Low-angle, compact limestone slabs situated directly along the approach path. Perfect for taking your very first steps on natural rock, learning friction climbing techniques on sloping footholds, and mastering top-rope belaying.
2. ÖAV Climbing Garden Martinswand: Maintained by the Austrian Alpine Club (ÖAV), this sector features roughly 50 immaculately bolted routes with top anchors, ranging between 10 and 25 meters in height. Grades span UIAA 3 to 6 (with about 15 routes in the gentle 3 to 4 range tailored for beginners and children). The solid Wetterstein limestone features positive ledges and cracks, though popular footholds are polished.
Taster classes generally run for 3 to 5 hours. The curriculum covers gear fitting, harness adjustment, tying in with a figure-eight knot, mandatory partner checks, and top-rope belay mechanics using modern assisted braking devices. No prior climbing experience is necessary; basic fitness and freedom from vertigo are sufficient. Suitable for adventurous kids aged 6 to 8 and above. Crucial safety rule: Due to the 600-meter wall towering overhead, climbing helmets are strictly mandatory for everyone at the base of the cliff (climbers, belayers, and observers) to protect against objective rockfall hazards. Dogs should not be brought to the crag base due to rockfall risks.

Getting There
The cliff sits right along the B171 highway between Innsbruck-Kranebitten and Zirl. From the primary parking area P1 (Martinsbühel, on the right just past the wastewater plant when coming from Innsbruck), a well-marked mountain path reaches the crag base in just 5 to 10 minutes. By public transit, regional VVT bus lines 4123 and 4176 run from Innsbruck directly to the Zirl Martinsbühel stop at the trailhead. Alternatively, take the S-Bahn train to Kematen in Tirol station (2.5 km by bike or local bus).

Tips
Boasting full southern exposure at 650 meters elevation, the Martinswand acts as a gigantic natural heat radiator in the Inntal valley. Climbing is possible year-round—mild winter days often allow taster sessions in T-shirts, whereas high summer demands early morning starts before the rock heats up. Instructional sessions are hosted regularly by the Innsbruck Alpine Club (from €80) and certified mountain schools (from €120 including harness, helmet, and belay device). Sticky climbing shoes can be rented from outdoor shops in Innsbruck. In case of sustained rain, courses easily relocate to the world-renowned Kletterzentrum Innsbruck (KI) climbing gym.
